correctness.rationale: Independently reconstruct the full range from frozen RESULT.md lines 7–11. End-of-day storage is always at most 3, so a dry day never meets demand and resets storage to zero. Both six-unit days meet demand. The low-rain day can become the third full day only immediately after a six: if that six is preceded by another six it leaves 3, otherwise the first six leaves 2 (the low-rain day is still ahead and the only remaining predecessor is the dry day). Thus the low-day thresholds are respectively z=1 and z=2; a first or post-dry low day is never full. In 1≤z<2 only (0,6,6,z) and (6,6,z,0) meet three full days. Each spills one unit on the second six; the former retains z−1 at the end and supplies 12, the latter drains on the final dry day and supplies 11+z. In particular the one-unit overflow in both is not a one-unit volume deficit in both. Conservation gives V≤12+z, attained for all z by (6,z,6,0), which has 2 full days before z=2 and 3 thereafter. For z<1 that order also attains the maximum of two full days, including the z=0 duplicate-rain case. This proves the exact window and both endpoint decisions without relying on rational sample points. value.rationale: The practical mathematical question is whether optimizing one standard reliability measure can serve as a proxy for optimizing the other on the same inflow data. This small exact counterexample makes that distinction auditable: it isolates how consecutive wet days trade spillage for a third full day, gives a nondegenerate sharp interval with different decisions at its two boundaries, and quantifies the best penalty. This is useful as an analytical benchmark for dual-criterion implementations and timing conventions, not as an instruction to reorder natural rainfall or a general sizing result.
